set.quote: A counterfactual explanation $\mathbf{x}_{\text{CE}}$ is a modified version of the original input $\mathbf{x}$ that would lead the model to change its decision, that is, $f(\mathbf{x})\neq f(\mathbf{x}_{\text{CE}})$ . (2017); Mothilal et al. (2020); Verma et al. (2024).

set.quote: The prover is said to be checkable if there exists a verifier $v$ such that the prover can always convince the verifier when its answer is correct, and there exists no adversarial proof that can trick the verifier into accepting an incorrect answer. Formally, • Completeness: $\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\mathds{1}_{\text{correct}}\left({x,\pi(x)}\right)=1\implies v(x,\pi(x))=1$ . • Soundness: $\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\forall z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z},\mathds{1}_{\text{correct}}\left({x,z^{\prime}}\right)=0\implies v(x,z^{\prime})=0$ .

add.quote: The probing results from all the token positions $t$ and layers $l$ are aggregated as follows: | | $\displaystyle t^{*}(v_{i})$ | $\displaystyle=\min\{t\mid\max_{l}\mathrm{acc}(t,l,v_{i})>\tau\}\text{,}$ | | (2) where $\mathrm{acc}(t,l,v_{i})\in[0,1]$ denotes the probing accuracy of $f_{t,l,v_{i}}$ . The position $t^{*}(v_{i})\in\mathbb{Z}$ indicates when the first time the probing classifier achieved a reasonable accuracy above $\tau$ . We set $\tau=0.9$ in our main experiment, and we show additional results with different thresholds in Appendix B.3. As a more coarse but comprehensive value, we also report $t_{\mathrm{eq}}^{*}(v_{i})$ , indicating which equation $t_{\mathrm{eq}}$ in the input $x$ the position $t^{*}(v_{i})$ falls into. Given that the $t$ (and $t_{\mathrm{eq}}$ ) is relative to the CoT-beginning position, if $t_{\mathrm{(eq)}}^{*}(v_{i})$ is negative, the value $\$\{v_{i}\}$ is computed before CoT begins.
add.gloss: First token position where some layer's probe decodes the (sub-)answer with accuracy above τ=0.9; negative t* means the value is computed before CoT, i.e. a predetermined answer.

add.quote: As complementary information of the position, we also report two types of accuracy: | | $\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{\prec CoT}}(v_{i})$ | $\displaystyle=\max_{t<0,l}\mathrm{acc}(t,l,v_{i})\text{,}$ | | (3) | | $\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{\succ CoT}}(v_{i})$ | $\displaystyle=\max_{t\geq 0,l}\mathrm{acc}(t,l,v_{i})\text{.}$ | | (4) If $\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{\prec CoT}}(v_{i})$ is sufficiently high, $\$\{v_{i}\}$ is resolved internally before CoT begins. Conversely, if $\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{\prec CoT}}(v_{i})$ is low and $\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{\succ CoT}}(v_{i})$ is high, the answer is derived while performing CoT reasoning.
add.gloss: Best probe accuracy before vs. after CoT starts; high pre-CoT accuracy means the answer was resolved before CoT, low pre- and high post-CoT means it is derived during CoT.

add.quote: We report Success Rate as a metric for this experiment. The Success rate indicates how frequently (%) the intervened output $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{patch}}$ aligns with the correct answer $\tilde{y}$ . For reasoning chains, we report the Success rate for $\hat{z_{t}}^{\mathrm{patch}}$ as well.

add.gloss: Share of patched runs whose output stays the original y; complements Success rate in locating which hidden states the answer causally depends on.

add.quote: The mitigation team aims to detect and mitigate steganographic communication of the payload by the collusion team. It consists of an overseer and an optional paraphraser. The paraphraser rewords the stegotext in an attempt to remove the payload.
add.gloss: Oversight side of the game: an overseer that flags suspicious stegotexts plus an optional paraphraser that rewrites them to strip any hidden payload.

add.quote: Single-episode LLM-logits Overseer (O1). A (white-box access) LLM is prompted to classify whether a single stegotext appears suspicious. We then use the logits for the Yes/No tokens, $z_{\text{Yes}}$ and $z_{\text{No}}$ , along with a sensitivity threshold $t_{\text{sens}}$ , to compute the suspiciousness score $r_{\text{sus}}$ for each stegotext: $r_{\text{sus}}=\tanh\left(z_{\text{Yes}}-z_{\text{No}}-t_{\text{sens}}\right)$ . Here, Overseer Bypass Success = $r_{\text{sus}}<t_{\text{sens}}$ .
add.gloss: White-box monitor: suspiciousness is tanh of the Yes-minus-No logit gap minus a calibrated threshold; a stegotext bypasses it when r_sus < t_sens.

add.quote: Multi-episode LLM-sampling Overseer (O2). A (black-box access) LLM is prompted to evaluate a batch of stegotexts to determine if they seem suspicious. The LLM returns a single yes/no answer for the entire batch, which is converted into a suspiciousness score as follows: $r_{\text{sus}}=1\text{ if "Yes"},0\text{ if "No"}$ . This $r_{\text{sus}}$ is then applied to each stegotext in the batch. Here, Overseer Bypass Success = 1 - $r_{\text{sus}}$ .
add.gloss: Black-box monitor gives one yes/no verdict for a whole batch of stegotexts; that binary score is applied to every item in the batch.

add.quote: Multi-episode LLM-sampling Thresholded Overseer (O3). A (black-box access) LLM is prompted to evaluate individual stegotexts within a batch to score their suspiciousness. It assigns a per-sample score between 0 and 5 to each stegotext (where 0 indicates harmless and 5 indicates highly suspicious). The entire batch is then assigned a binary $r_{\text{sus}}$ score if more than $T_{n}$ % of the samples have a per-sample score greater than or equal to a threshold $T_{s}$ . This $r_{\text{sus}}$ is then applied to each stegotext in the batch. Here, Overseer Bypass Success = 1 - $r_{\text{sus}}$ .
add.gloss: Monitor rates each stegotext 0-5; the batch is flagged if more than T_n% of items score at least T_s. Thresholds are calibrated on honest runs (App. D.1).

add.quote: Standard Paraphraser (SP). An LLM is passed the stegotext and asked to re-word it (Roger and Greenblatt, 2023).
add.gloss: Mitigation against encoded payloads: an LLM rewords the stegotext.

add.quote: Context-aware Paraphraser (CAP). An LLM is passed the stegotext, along with details regarding the task the sender should perform. It is asked to reword the stegotext while removing any details irrelevant to the task (Roger and Greenblatt, 2023).
add.gloss: Paraphraser that also sees the sender's task and removes task-irrelevant details, the stronger defense against multi-bit encodings in the paper's results.

add.quote: Coding Paraphraser (CP). In coding tasks, we make use of non-LLM paraphraser which deterministically processes the sender’s output, renaming all variables to generic names and removing all comments.
add.gloss: Deterministic code normalizer used as a steganography mitigation: renames all variables to generic names and strips comments.

add.quote: (2) Decoding Success: Receiver successfully decodes the payload.
add.gloss: Rate at which the receiver recovers the hidden payload; in the mitigation tasks it is the collusion team's task reward.

add.quote: In addition to using an overseer that looks for steganography in the stegotext, we also flag a batch of stegotexts as suspicious if the Sender Task Success falls below a certain Honest-Performance threshold (refer to Appendix D.1 for details). Thus, here collusion is successful (i.e., Collusion Success) when: (i) the stegotext is suitably performant, (ii) the receiver correctly decodes the payload, and (iii) the stegotext is not flagged as suspicious by the overseer.
add.gloss: Collusion succeeds only if the stegotext still does its task, the payload is decoded, and the overseer does not flag it; low task performance is itself flagged as suspicious.

add.quote: We say that a set of episodes are suspicious if: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}{p_{i}}>T_{p}$ where $n$ is the number of episodes and $T_{p}$ is a performance threshold, or $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}{[s\geq T_{s}]}>T_{n}$ where $T_{s}$ is a suspiciousness level threshold and $T_{n}$ is a threshold on the proportion of suspicous episodes.
add.gloss: Batch flagged if task performance falls below T_p (90% of honest; printed formula reads >) or if over T_n of episodes score at least T_s; thresholds from honest runs.

add.quote: We define the "Useful safety factor" as the fractional drop in task performance which is allowed before a set of episodes is judged to be suspicious. If the task performance is $1.0$ , a useful safety factor of $0.1$ would lead to a task performance threshold of $0.9$ .
add.gloss: Allowed fractional drop in task performance before a batch is judged suspicious; 0.1 in the main experiments.

add.quote: We define the "Suspiciuosness safety factor" as the multiplier on the allowed number of suspicious episodes, when compared to the honest evaluations. If $10$ episodes are flagged as suspicious in the honest evaluations, then a safety factor of $2$ means any set of episodes with over $20$ suspicious messages will be judged as suspicious.
add.gloss: Multiplier on the number of suspicious episodes seen in honest runs that a batch may reach before being flagged; 2 in the main experiments.

add.quote: Without using the sensitive variables, the maximum task success that can be achieved on the historic dataset is Max-Clean-Success < 67%. add.gloss: Under a misspecified reward plus an overseer penalty, optimization makes the behavior harder to detect rather than removing it; the paper's GBRL-SB runs show this for collusion.

set.quote: We frame steganography as an adversarial relationship between two teams, a collusion team and a mitigation team. The collusion team consists of a sender and a receiver, and aims to complete a task $t$ while communicating a secret payload $p$ . The sender sends a message to the receiver called the stegotext, within which it hides the payload.

add.term: adding mistakes / paraphrasing / filler tokens (Lanham et al. tests)
add.quote: Similarly, if adding mistakes in a generated CoT causes the model to change its final response, then the original CoT can be considered faithful. Analogously, they proposed other metrics to measure faithfulness based on paraphrasing the beginning portions of the original CoT as well as replacing the CoT with filler tokens (e.g., ellipses).
add.gloss: Restates Lanham et al.: a CoT counts as faithful if inserting mistakes changes the answer; further tests paraphrase the early CoT or replace it with filler tokens.

add.term: faithful reasoning chain (solver-answer match, Lyu et al.)
add.quote: For example, Lyu et al. [18] focused on generating a reasoning chain that could then be put through a deterministic math solver, and the resulting answer from this solver was compared to the answer produced by the LLM. The reasoning chain was considered to be faithful if the answers of the solver and the LLM matched.
add.gloss: Restated Lyu et al. criterion: chain faithful if a deterministic solver run on it gives the LLM's answer. The paper rejects it as not capturing the LLM's internal computation.

add.term: unfaithful CoT via unmentioned biasing inputs (Turpin et al.)
add.quote: Turpin et al. [22] were the first to demonstrate that CoT explanations may not faithfully capture the behavior of the underlying models. They showed that these explanations can be heavily influenced by biasing model inputs e.g., by reordering multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to always make the answer “(A)”—which these models systematically fail to mention in their explanations.
add.gloss: CoT explanations are swayed by biasing input features, such as always-(A) answer orderings, that the explanations never mention.

set.quote: Specifically, we employ the Early Answering strategy, which evaluates the faithfulness of a CoT by sequentially adding each CoT step to the question and querying the LLM for its answer, conditioned on the truncated set of CoT steps. If the answer from the LLM converges towards the final answer as it encounters more CoT steps, it indicates that the CoT explanation is guiding the answer and is more likely to be faithful.
